blocks.text: Richard was a little late in the morning, but I did not have to wait for him long. We turned into the park. The air was bright and fresh with dew, and there was not a cloud in the sky. The birds sang beautifully. The ferns, the grass and the trees sparkled, and it was wonderful to see. The woods seemed twenty times richer than they had been yesterday. In the still night they had looked so heavy and silent, as if they were deeply asleep. But it seemed that Nature had been more awake than usual all night. She had worked on every tiny detail of every wonderful leaf, to make that day glorious.
“This is a lovely place,” said Richard, looking round. “There is none of the harsh noise and quarrelling of law-suits here!”
But there was other trouble.
“I'll tell you what, my dear girl,” said Richard. “When I have settled my affairs in general, I think I shall come down here and rest.”
“Would it not be better to rest now?” I asked.
“Oh, as for resting now,” said Richard, “or doing anything very definite now, that's not easy. In short, it can't be done. I can't do it, at least.”
“Why not?” said I.

“You know why not, Esther. Imagine that you were living in an unfinished house. At any time, someone might put the roof on or take it off. The whole house might be pulled down or built up, from top to bottom. It could happen tomorrow, or the next day, or next week, or next month, or next year. You would find it hard to rest or settle down. So do I. Now? There's no ‘now’ for us suitors—for us people with a case in the court.”

Then I saw the same dark look on his face that I had seen last night. When I saw it, I could almost believe in the strange attraction that my poor little wandering friend had talked about at such length. It was terrible to think, but the look also had in it a hint of that unfortunate man who had died.
“My dear Richard,” said I, “this is a bad beginning of our conversation.”
“I knew you would tell me so, Dame Durden.”
“And I am not the only one who says so, dear Richard. Someone else once warned you never to build any hope or expectation on the family curse. It was not I.”

“There you go, back to John Jarndyce!” said Richard impatiently. “Well! We must come to him sooner or later, because he is the main thing I have to talk about. So we may as well do it at once. My dear Esther, how can you be so blind? Don't you see that he is an interested party? He has something to gain or lose in the case himself. It may suit him very well if I know nothing about the suit and care nothing about it. But it may not suit me quite so well.”

“O Richard,” I protested. “You have seen him and heard him. You have lived in his house and known him. How is it possible that you can still have such unworthy suspicions? How can you even whisper them, even to me, in this lonely place where no one can hear us?”
He turned deep red, as if his natural generosity felt a sharp sting of blame. He was silent for a little while. Then he answered in a quiet voice:
“Esther, I am sure you know that I am not a mean fellow. And I do understand, to some degree, that suspicion and distrust are poor qualities in someone of my age.”
“I know it very well,” said I. “I am not more sure of anything.”

“That's a dear girl!” Richard answered quickly, “and that's just like you, because it gives me comfort. I needed to get some little bit of comfort out of all this business. It's a bad business even at its best, as I don't need to tell you.”

“I know it perfectly,” said I. “I know, Richard—what shall I say?—I know as well as you do that such wrong ideas about people are not part of your true nature. And I know, as well as you know, what is changing your nature so much.”

“Come, sister, come,” said Richard, a little more cheerfully. “In any case, you will be fair with me. If I have the bad luck to be under that influence, so has he. If it has twisted me a little, it may have twisted him a little, too. Apart from all this confusion and uncertainty, I don't say that he is not an honorable man. I am sure he is. But it spoils everybody. You know it spoils everybody. You have heard him say so fifty times. Then why should he escape?”
